title: Rejected Twice by the Academy, He Ended Up Sculpting Both Sides of Hungary's History
standfirst: Endre Bartos never passed the entrance exam at Hungary's Academy of Fine Arts. He spent two decades painting around municipal day jobs, was pensioned off in 1977 over his failing eyesight, and became, in the years after, the sculptor his hometown trusted to commemorate — within two years of each other — the men executed for rebelling against the Habsburgs and the family that executed them.

sections.heading: The Year His Eyes Failed Was the Year He Became a Painter
sections.body:
Endre Bartos spent a decade clocking in at the gasworks in Baja, the small Danube town where he was born in 1930 and would die in 2006. He had been painting the whole time — his first solo show went up in the town in 1972, five years into that job — but it was still something he did around a shift, not instead of one. That changed in 1977, when his eyesight failed badly enough that the state certified him disabled and he left the gasworks for good.

The following year is the year of this canvas. It is also the year [Bács-Kiskun county gave Bartos its own art prize](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartos_Endre), the first official recognition of a career that had, until then, existed mostly on evenings and weekends. No source ties this specific painting to that specific prize — nothing that direct is on the record — but the two dates sit next to each other in a way that is hard to read as accident: a man whose working eyes had just been taken from one job spent the following year being taken seriously, for the first time, in the other one.

sections.heading: Rejected by the Academy of Fine Arts — More Than Once
sections.body:
Bartos applied repeatedly to Hungary's Academy of Fine Arts in Budapest and was turned down every time. His only formal training was a horticultural school; everything after that he taught himself. It did not stop him working around institutions rather than through them: a stint in Budapest's city planning office, a return to Baja in 1954 for a post in the district council's cultural department, then six years, from 1962 to 1967, running the equivalent department in nearby Szeged. In 1967 he came back to Baja again and took the gasworks job that would occupy him for the next decade.

None of that is unusual for a provincial arts career built without academic backing. What is unusual is how much institutional trust he was given anyway, later, in a country whose museums generally decide who gets to make public monuments. By the time he had a body of work behind him, Bartos was the town's default answer to who should make a memorial — the [Hungarian military history museum and the Museum of Medical History](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartos_Endre) eventually held dozens of his portrait medals and reliefs, from a man with no art school on his record at all.

sections.heading: The Exact Spot Where a Hungarian King Left for Good
sections.body:
Baja is not a random place for a Habsburg memorial. On 31 October 1921, King Charles IV — the last Habsburg to sit on the Hungarian throne — boarded a ship at the Danube bridgehead in Baja and left Hungarian soil for the last time, bound for exile on Madeira. The town later built [a stone staircase down to the water](https://intezet.nori.gov.hu/tortenelmi-emlekhelyek/baja/baja-iv-karoly-lepcso) and named it for him; its inscription, replaced after decades of neglect, records that he left his homeland here for an exile forced on him by his enemies.

Bartos was born in that town nine years after Charles IV's departure, into a place where the end of the monarchy was not an abstraction from a textbook but a specific set of steps by the river that everyone in Baja could point to. Decades later, when the town wanted a memorial to the king who had left from that exact spot, it turned to its own self-taught sculptor rather than importing one from Budapest.

sections.heading: Seventy Years Later, the King's Son Came Back to Unveil It
sections.body:
On 1 November 1991, [Otto von Habsburg](https://intezet.nori.gov.hu/tortenelmi-emlekhelyek/baja/baja-iv-karoly-lepcso) — Charles IV's son, by then in his late seventies and long since reinvented as a European parliamentarian rather than a pretender to any throne — spent two days in Baja. The occasion was the unveiling of a memorial by Bartos to Charles IV and Queen Zita, [installed near the Hotel Sugovica](https://intezet.nori.gov.hu/tortenelmi-emlekhelyek/baja/baja-iv-karoly-lepcso) by the same river his father had left from seventy years before.

It is a strange kind of commission for an artist twice rejected by the national academy: sculpting the likenesses of a deposed king and queen well enough that their own son would travel to a small provincial town to unveil them, the work [catalogued today among Bartos's public monuments](https://www.kozterkep.hu/alkotok/megtekintes/3580/bartos-endre) alongside memorials to the people that same royal house had once executed for treason.

sections.heading: Two Years Earlier: Faces for the Men the Habsburgs Hanged
sections.body:
In 1989, the year Communist rule ended in Hungary, Bartos completed a memorial in Baja to the martyrs of Arad: [fifteen portrait reliefs arranged in a circle](https://www.kozterkep.hu/3294/aradi-vertanuk-emlekmuve), among them Lajos Batthyány, Hungary's first constitutional prime minister, and the thirteen honvéd officers executed alongside him after the failed [1848–49 war of independence against Habsburg rule](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Az_aradi_v%C3%A9rtan%C3%BAk_eml%C3%A9kezete). Lines from a nineteenth-century poem by Lajos Palágyi run around the memorial, framing the executions as a lesson the nation is bound to keep relearning.

Bartos went on to build variations on the same theme through the 1990s — a combined Batthyány-and-martyrs memorial in Kiskunhalas in 1999, another set of thirteen reliefs in Csávoly that same year. In the space of a decade, the same hand sculpted both the men Vienna had executed for rebelling against it and the family that had ordered the executions. It is a commission list that only makes sense in a country working through an entire, contradictory nineteenth and twentieth century at once, in public, right after the fall of Communism — and in Baja, at least, it landed on a painter with no formal art training at all.

sections.heading: Seven Hundred Faces, Under an Hour Each
sections.body:
For all the monument work, painting remained Bartos's main output, and portraits dominated it: sources credit him with [around 700 of them](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartos_Endre), always from a live sitter, each finished in a single session of under an hour. Hungarian sources describing his landscapes call them derűs, mint a magyar nyár — [cheerful, like a Hungarian summer](https://budapestaukcio.hu/bartos-endre/festo) — which makes this one, an autumn forest, something of an exception within an already minor part of his output.

The forest itself was not incidental. Bartos said the floodplain woods beside his hometown had been decisive for him and had held, for decades, the single most important place among his subjects. Of the roughly fifty works of his that survive in [public image databases today](https://www.wikiart.org/en/endre-bartos), only a handful are landscapes at all — most of what got photographed and catalogued down the years was the portraits, not the trees he kept returning to on his own account.

sections.heading: Filed Under a Word His Own Listing Doesn't Use
sections.body:
This corpus records Autumn forest under Fauvism. That is not what anyone closer to the source calls it. [WikiArt's own page for this exact painting](https://www.wikiart.org/en/endre-bartos/autumn-forest-1978) lists its style as Expressionism, not Fauvism. [Kieselbach, the Budapest auction house](https://www.kieselbach.hu/artist/bartos_-endre_7466) that maintains his artist file, describes him only as a self-taught painter and medal artist. The [Hungarian Wikipedia entry on Bartos](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartos_Endre) uses one word for his style — expresszionista, bright coloring, direct expression of personality — and never mentions Fauvism, in relation to this work or any other in his catalogue.

None of that makes Fauvism indefensible as a loose stylistic cousin — bright, non-naturalistic color is exactly what both movements shared. But it is a label imported from French art history onto a self-taught Hungarian painter who never trained in Paris, never showed there, and whose own country's sources describe him in a different, adjacent word. Filed one way here, described another way everywhere else — a fair summary, in the end, of a career built entirely outside the institutions that do the filing.
